front_blocks.md: Define the term **anion**.

back_blocks.md: An **anion** is a negatively charged ion. In qualitative analysis, common anions tested for include carbonate (CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2-</sup>), halide (Cl<sup>-</sup>, Br<sup>-</sup>, I<sup>-</sup>) and sulfate (SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup>) ions.

front_blocks.md: What are the **reagent** and **result** for the test for **carbonate ions**?

back_blocks.md: Add dilute acid to the sample — effervescence occurs. Bubble the gas produced through **limewater**. A positive result is limewater turning **cloudy white**, indicating carbon dioxide is present.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Dilute hydrochloric acid should be used to acidify a sample before testing for halide ions.
**(Extended Tier Only)**

back_blocks.md: **False.**
**Dilute nitric acid** must be used. Hydrochloric acid contains chloride ions (Cl<sup>-</sup>) which would react with silver nitrate and give a false positive result for chloride.

front_blocks.md: What colours are the precipitates formed when silver nitrate is added to solutions of Cl<sup>-</sup>, Br<sup>-</sup> and I<sup>-</sup>?
**(Extended Tier Only)**

back_blocks.md:
1. Cl<sup>-</sup>: **white** precipitate (silver chloride)
2. Br<sup>-</sup>: **cream** precipitate (silver bromide)
3. I<sup>-</sup>: **yellow** precipitate (silver iodide)

front_blocks.md: Why is **nitric acid** added before **barium nitrate** in the test for sulfate ions?

back_blocks.md: **Nitric acid** is added first to remove any **carbonate** ions present. Carbonate ions would also produce a white precipitate with barium nitrate, which could give a false positive result for sulfate.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
A white precipitate forms when barium nitrate is added to a solution containing sulfate ions.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
Barium nitrate reacts with sulfate ions to form **barium sulfate**, which is an insoluble white precipitate.

front_blocks.md: What is the **ionic equation** for the formation of the precipitate in the test for sulfate ions?

back_blocks.md: Ba<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup> (aq) → BaSO<sub>4</sub> (s)
Barium ions react with sulfate ions to form **insoluble barium sulfate**, which appears as a white precipitate.

front_blocks.md: How can you distinguish between **bromide ions** and **iodide ions** using silver nitrate solution?
**(Extended Tier Only)**

back_blocks.md: Add dilute nitric acid then silver nitrate solution. Bromide ions give a **cream** precipitate (silver bromide), while iodide ions give a **yellow** precipitate (silver iodide). The different colours allow them to be distinguished.

front_blocks.md: What is the test for **ammonium ions** and what is the positive result?

back_blocks.md: Gently warm the solution with **sodium hydroxide solution**. A positive result is that the gas produced turns damp **red litmus paper blue**, confirming the presence of **ammonia** gas.

front_blocks.md: Describe a **flame test** for metal cations.

back_blocks.md: A **flame test** involves cleaning a nichrome or platinum wire loop, dipping it into the sample, then holding it in the blue Bunsen flame. The colour of the flame identifies the metal cation present.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
The white precipitate of zinc hydroxide dissolves when excess sodium hydroxide solution is added.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
Zn<sup>2+</sup> forms a white precipitate with a few drops of NaOH. The precipitate **dissolves** in excess NaOH to form a **colourless solution**.

front_blocks.md: What colours are the precipitates formed when sodium hydroxide is added dropwise to solutions of Fe<sup>2+</sup> and Fe<sup>3+</sup>?

back_blocks.md: Fe<sup>2+</sup> gives a **green** precipitate (iron(II) hydroxide). Fe<sup>3+</sup> gives a **red-brown** precipitate (iron(III) hydroxide). Both precipitates do not dissolve in excess sodium hydroxide.

front_blocks.md: In a flame test, **sodium** ions give a **..........**  flame, **potassium** ions give a **..........**  flame, and **copper** ions give a **..........**  flame.

back_blocks.md: In a flame test, **sodium** ions give a **yellow** flame, **potassium** ions give a **lilac** flame, and **copper** ions give a **blue-green** flame.

front_blocks.md: How does excess **ammonia solution** help distinguish Cu<sup>2+</sup> from Ca<sup>2+</sup>?

back_blocks.md: With excess ammonia solution, the **light blue precipitate** of copper(II) hydroxide dissolves to give a **dark blue solution**. The white precipitate of calcium hydroxide does not dissolve in excess ammonia.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Lithium ions produce a red flame in a flame test.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
Li<sup>+</sup> ions give a **red** flame. Each metal cation produces its own characteristic flame colour, which is what makes the flame test useful for identification.

front_blocks.md: Why must sodium hydroxide solution be added **slowly and dropwise** when testing for metal cations?

back_blocks.md: Adding NaOH slowly prevents the precipitate from dissolving in **excess** before it can be observed. Zinc hydroxide dissolves in excess NaOH, so adding it too quickly could cause you to miss the **precipitate** forming.

front_blocks.md: How do you distinguish **Ca**<sup>**2+**</sup> from **Zn**<sup>**2+**</sup> using sodium hydroxide solution?

back_blocks.md: Both Ca<sup>2+</sup> and Zn<sup>2+</sup> form white precipitates with a few drops of NaOH. Adding **excess** NaOH distinguishes them: the zinc hydroxide precipitate **dissolves** to form a colourless solution, while the calcium hydroxide precipitate **does not dissolve**.

front_blocks.md: How do you distinguish between **hydrogen** and **oxygen** when testing with a splint?

back_blocks.md: Use a **burning (lighted) splint** for hydrogen — it gives a squeaky pop. Use a **glowing splint** for oxygen — it relights. The splint type (burning vs glowing) is the key difference.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
A burning splint that is extinguished confirms the presence of carbon dioxide.

back_blocks.md: **False.**

Extinguishing a burning splint is not a definitive test for carbon dioxide — other gases such as nitrogen will also do this. The correct test is to bubble the gas through **limewater**, which turns cloudy white only in the presence of CO<sub>2</sub>.

front_blocks.md: Describe the test for **hydrogen gas**.

back_blocks.md: Hold a **burning (lighted) splint** at the open end of the test tube containing the gas. **Hydrogen** burns with a loud **squeaky pop**, caused by the rapid combustion of hydrogen with oxygen to form water.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
The test for chlorine uses damp red litmus paper, which turns blue.
**(Extended Tier Only)**

back_blocks.md: **False.**
The test for **chlorine** uses damp **blue** litmus paper (not red). Chlorine first turns it red (due to acid formation), then **bleaches it white**. Ammonia, not chlorine, turns red litmus blue.

front_blocks.md: Why does **chlorine** gas turn damp blue litmus paper red before bleaching it white?
**(Extended Tier Only)**

back_blocks.md: When chlorine dissolves in water, it forms acidic products (including **hydrochloric acid** and hypochlorous acid). These acids turn the litmus red. The chlorine then **bleaches** the litmus white by oxidising the dye.

front_blocks.md: What is the difference between **ammonium ions** (NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>) and **ammonia gas** (NH<sub>3</sub>) in the context of gas tests?

back_blocks.md: **Ammonium ions** (NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>) are aqueous cations present in solution. **Ammonia gas** (NH<sub>3</sub>) is the gas released when ammonium ions are warmed with sodium hydroxide. The gas test uses damp red litmus paper, which turns blue in the presence of NH<sub>3</sub>.
